transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: There is a famous story about Henry Ford, the man who made cars affordable for everyone. He believed it was wasteful for any part of a car to last longer than the car itself. He even sent workers to car junkyards to find parts that were too strong, so that he could make them cheaper in the future. For Ford, a car was a simple machine: when one part stopped working, you bought a new car.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ford's thinking is useful when we look at electric cars today. Many people believe that EV batteries get old quickly and stop working well. Because of this, they think it is better to buy a new car than a used one. This idea is one reason why electric cars lose their value faster than petrol or diesel cars. Worried that the battery will die, many buyers stay away from used electric cars.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: There is good news on price, however. Building batteries is now 99 per cent cheaper than it was 30 years ago. Even so, the battery still makes up about a third of the price of a new electric car. Cheaper batteries mean cheaper cars, and that makes a real difference. That is why this month's news was welcome: in the UK, the average new electric car now costs less than the average new petrol car.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: But what about the battery itself? A recent report found that EV batteries, if they are looked after well, should actually last longer than the cars themselves. In other words, used electric cars are a much better deal than most people think. The battery you worry about may well outlive the car around it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: These are not the only reasons why electric cars are becoming more attractive, whether new or used. Because electric cars sit parked and plugged in for almost 23 hours every day, their batteries are available to store power even when the car is not being driven. Companies now plan to tap those batteries to store extra electricity for the national energy system, and when the system needs it back, the owners get paid. The idea is not new, but a trial in the United States now shows how profitable it could be: the average driver could earn several thousand pounds a year. For many families, that is a serious amount of money.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: So it may be money, not the climate, that finally convinces people to go electric. Home charging is usually much cheaper than filling a petrol tank, so running an electric car costs less. Fuel prices are another factor: the war in Iran has made petrol more expensive, which may push more people towards electric cars. And although the EV industry has seen slower sales recently, lower prices and cheaper running costs make the future for electric cars more certain.
